encodingDesc.p: This document is a simplified "true-to-text" XML version of The Spanish Curate based on Pennsylvania State University's annotated copy of the 1647 Beaumont & Fletcher first folio. Major textual elements and attributes have been captured based on how they appear in the folio. Whenever possible, editorial interventions have been minimalized or avoided entirely. This document is meant to serve as a pedagogical tool by which students of Early Modern literature can learn to construct edited XML versions of the play.

projectDesc.p: The Digital Beaumont & Fletcher (1647) is a collaborative editorial project aimed at making many of the rarely edited—and, as a result, rarely taught—plays in the “Beaumont & Fletcher” canon accessible to student readers and freely available online for classroom use. This project was inspired by the distinctive copy of Comedies and Tragedies Written by Francis Beavmont And Iohn Fletcher Gentlemen (1647) held by Penn State University's Eberly Family Special Collections Library. In addition to preserving evidence of ownership dating to as early as 1703, Penn State's copy of this printed play collection also includes three plays with handwritten marginalia, suggesting that the book might have been used to facilitate performance in the late seventeenth century. This project is also motivated by a desire to make the texts and other features of this book more widely known and readable. As a first step, the whole volume has now been fully digitized, thanks to the department of Preservation, Conservation, and Digitization at Penn State Libraries.

Only a dish to every man I have dedicated,

For me some forty pound of lovely beef,

You shall be bobbed, (gentlemen),
Stir, and as I have a life, ye go to prison.

That comes to tell ye a delightfull story
Of an old whore ye have and then to teach ye
What is the penalty. Laugh at me now, sir,

(And pay it on the nail)? To fly my fury?
Oh, gentle sir.
Do'st thou hope I will be gentle,
Thou foolish, inconsiderate Curate?
Let me go, sir.
I'll see thee hang first.

Hark in your ear hark softly—
No, no bribery.

Mockt me abominably; abused me lewdly.

And groan, and die indeed, and be worth nothing
Not worth a blessing, nor a bell to knell to knell: bell's tolling for thee,

Stealest from the Merchant, and the ring he was buried with

For some near reasons, that concerns my credit,

Do sir, and spare not.

She has, yes, and too worthy of your usage.

And turn that man, that dares but taint her virtues,

A gentleman, a free man.

Yo know my name indeed. I am now no Lawyer.

Immediately take honest and fair truce

I shall not trouble ye.
We will be friends, too.

I grant ye.

lg.l: Why do'st thou follow me?
To save your life.
A plot is laid for't, all my wrongs forgot,
I have a brother's love.Manuscript note: Le: Mill: ar: bar be ready
But thy false self,
I fear no enemy.
You have no friend
But what breaths in me. If you move a step
Beyond this ground you tread on you are lost.
'Tis by thy practice then: I am sent hither
To meet her that prefers my life and safety
Before her own.
That you should be abused 'thus
With weak credulity weak credulity: false belief. She, for whose sake
You have forgot we had one noble father,
Or that one mother bare us. For whose love
You break a contract to which heaven was witness,
To satisfy whose pride, and willful humour,
You have exposed a sweet and hopeful son,
To all the miseries that want can bring him.
And such a son, though you are the most obdurate obdurate: hardened,
To give whom entertainment savages
Would quit their caves caves: homes themselves, to keep him from
Bleak cold and hunger. This dissembling dissembling: deceiving woman,
This idol, whom you worship: all your love
And service trod under her feet, designs you
To fill a grave or dead to lie a pray,
For wolves and vultures.
'Tis false; I defy thee,
And stand upon my guard.Manuscript note: Cross-hatched lines.

lg.l: Alas, 'tis weak:
Come on, since you will teach me to be cruel,
By having no faith in me, take your fortune:
Bring the rest forth, and bind bind: tie them fast.

lg.l: My Lord.
In what have we offended?
I am deaf deaf: numb,
And following my will, I do not stand Manuscript note: Violante be ready
Accomptable Accomptable: Accountable to reason. See her ring: Jamie shows Henrique Violante's ring.
(The first pledge of your love, and service to her),
Delivered as a warrant for your death.
These bags of gold you gave up to her trust
(The use of which, you did deny yourself),
Bestowed on me, and with a prodigal prodigal: reckless hand,
Whom she picked forth to be the architect architect: planner
Of her most bloody building building: plan; and to see
These instruments, to bring material
To raise it up, she bad me spare no cost.
And, (as a surplusage surplusage: bonus), offered herself
To be at my devotion.
Oh, accursed accursed: damnable!
But be incredulous still; think this my plot.
Fashion excuses to yourself, and swear
That she is innocent, that she doats on ye.
Believe this, as a fearful dream, and that
You lie not at my mercy, which in this
I will show only. She herself shall give
The dreadful sentence, to remove all scruple scruple: doubt

lg.l: Appeares my Violante? Speak, (my dearest).
Does not the object object: scene please you?
More than if
All treasure that's above the earth, with that,
That lies concealed in both the Indian mines,
Were laid down at my feet. Oh, bold Jamie,
Thou only canst deserve me.
I am forward.
And, (as you easily may perceive), I sleep not
On your commands.
But yet they live: I looked
To find them dead.
That was deferred deferred: delayed, that you
Might triumph in their misery, and have the power
To say they are not.
'Twas well thought upon.
This kiss, and all the pleasures of my bed
This night, shall thank thee.
Monster!
You sir, that
Would have me mother bastards, being unable
To honour me with one child of mine own.
That underneath my roof kept your cast-strumpet cast-strumpet: Violante is referring to Jacinta as a discarded prostitute.,
And out of my revenues would maintain
Her riotous issue riotous issue: troublesome child. Now you find what 'tis
To tempt a woman: with as little feeling
As I turn off a slave, that is unfit
To do me service; of a horse, or dog
That have out-lived their use, I shake thee off,
To make thy peace with heaven.
I do deserve this.
And never truly felt before what sorrow
Attends on willful dotage.
For you, mistress,
That had the pleasure of his youth before me,
And triumphed in the fruit that you had by him.
But that I think, to have the bastard strangled
Before thy face, and thou with speed to follow
The way he leads thee, is sufficent torture.
I would cut off thy nose, put out thine eyes,
And set my foot on these bewitching lips,
That had the start of mine. But as thou art;
Go to the grave unpitied.
Who would believe
Such rage could be in woman?
For this fellow: Gestures to Octavio.
He is not worth my knowledge.
Let him live then,
Since you esteem him innocent.
No, Jamie,
He shall make up the mess. Now strike together,
And let them fall so.
Unheard of cruelty!
I can endure no longer. Seize on her.
Am I betrayed?
Is this thy faith, Jamie?
Could your desires
Challenge performance of a deed so horrid?
Or, though that you had sold yourself to hell,
I should make up the bargain? Live, (dear brother),
Live long, and happy: I forgive you freely.
To have done you this service, is to me
A fair inheritance. And how e're harsh language

In my heart, I ever loved you. All my labours

These are the murderers, my noble friends,

I am too full

Were it but possible

That's my only comfort

All is come out,

Most gladly.
Your brother hath deserved well.

I have heart, advocate,

I'll change my copy.
